note:
THE PAPER COMES BACK. Vol. II No. 5 again — the source visibly repeats the January number and corpus.json preserves it — printed on the newsprint the 03-25 Extra said would arrive with the first vessels, four pages of six columns and 4,234 transcribed lines. Pages 1 and 2 are the Democratic meetings of April and May reprinted from four counties and the national canvass; pages 3 and 4 are the town: the editor's own 'CHICAGO' column, the advertising, the Chicago letter list of 31 March 1835, and the canal act on page 4.

THE MONTH'S CENTREPIECE IS THE LETTER LIST AND RULING 1 APPLIES IN FULL. It is Chicago's own post office — 'Cook Co., Illinois, on the 31st day of March, 1835' — so every listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged `letter_list_only`. 257 names are minted at c013 and how they were read out of two interleaved printed sub-columns is set out in that claim's note, including the twenty-five entries this pass refused to mint.

AND THE ADVERTISING PLACES STOREFRONTS. Nine of the twelve business claims here carry a `relative` or `corner` placement — Curtiss first door west of Jones, King & Co.; Collins & Caton two doors east of the Baptist Church; Hogan one door below the Post Office; Montgomery next door to P. Cohen's; Taylor a few rods north of Newberry & Dole's; Wilson next door to the city boot, shoe and leather store; the tinner at the corner of Dearborn and Lake; Spring first door north of the Tremont House; and the Democrat itself over Jones & King. That is the raw material T-0263 and T-0306 need and it is the reason this issue is worth its length.

claims.notes:
THE STATE OF THE TOWN'S SURFACE, SIX WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, from the man who walked it. Three facts a reconstruction can use and none of them flattering: GUTTERS exist and are not draining; the VACANT LOTS between and around the buildings hold sunken water-filled spots; and there is NOT ONE FIRE BUCKET in Chicago. The last is the strongest — a bare negative assertion about the town's equipment, hedged only by 'so far as we are advised', printed by a resident editor who would be contradicted in a week if he were wrong.

IT GETS WORSE BEFORE IT IS ACTED ON. The 1835-06-17 issue repeats the complaint in far stronger terms (barrels of putrid meat in a building in the most populous quarter; 'Our streets would disgrace a piggery') and the town meeting at the Presbyterian church that same week resolves to have the Trustees cleanse the streets. So the condition described here is the condition through May and June 1835, not a passing complaint. 'new buildings and new business' in the first sentence is the other half of the same picture and agrees with the Lake House and Rezigue-house notices of June.

claims.notes:
THE DEMOCRAT'S OWN SHOP, AND WHERE IT STOOD. The placement is NOT in this advertisement — it is in the paper's colophon on page 4 column 6, lines 4177-4180: 'Is published every W[ednesday] […] Chicago, Cook co. Ill. […] over Meserg Jones & King Hard[ware]'. Jones, King & Co.'s own advertisement of 1835-05-26 has them 'receiving by Brig Illinois' a hardware and stove stock, and J. Curtiss's advertisement puts Jones, King & Co. on SOUTH WATER STREET ('Office in South Water-street, first [door] west of Messrs. Jones, King & Co.'). So the Democrat was printed in an upper room over a South Water Street hardware store, which is a placeable workshop and not just a masthead. The street is carried on that chain and the anchor text is quoted from the colophon rather than invented.

WHAT THE SHOP WANTED. An apprentice printer in May and, from 1835-05-25, 'A FIRST rate BAKER; one who is well acquainted with the business' — the baker advertisement also says 'Enquire at this office', which is the paper acting as an employment exchange for somebody else, not baking. It is not read as the Democrat's own trade.

claims.notes:
THE PEOPLE OF CHICAGO ON 31 MARCH 1835, AS THE POST OFFICE HAD THEM — the densest record of who was here that this corpus holds for the three months before the scene date, and RULING 1 APPLIES IN FULL: this is Chicago's own office ('Cook Co, Illinois'), so every listed name mints a resident candidate and every entity here carries `letter_list_only`.

HOW THE LIST WAS READ, because it was not simply transcribed. The printed list runs in TWO narrow sub-columns inside one segmented column, A–H on the left and K–W on the right, and the segmenter has woven them line by line: line 2705 is 'Allger, William Kent, Alexander:C,' and is two people, not one. The boundary was found for each line and the two halves separated; where the automatic boundary was wrong it was corrected by hand line by line and the correction is recorded in the tool that built this claim. `lines_of_claim` names only the lines a name was read from, so the quote is exactly the list and not the column.

THE COUNT, STATED. 257 names minted. TWENTY-FIVE further half-lines were NOT minted and this is why: eight are the alphabet's own section letters standing alone ('A,', 'BR.', 'GC', 'H.', 'KF.', 'M-', 'N,', 'W,'); fourteen are OCR debris or a fragment with no recoverable surname ('emt, Sarah', 'oy, Orenge', 'iain, dohn 8', 'Ese cil, Archibald', '{Low af Whittier', 'd G. Sesotler'); two are truncated at the column edge ('Whi', 'Hallam. 3,11.'); and one, 'Dunham, ai. A', has a surname but no readable forename. Refusing them is the point: 257 is what the transcription supports and NOT necessarily what was printed. Twenty-six of the 257 carry an `[uncertain: …]` inside their normalized reading because the printed form will not resolve to a name with confidence, and those are minted with the doubt attached rather than smoothed into a plausible name.

WHAT THE LIST IS AND IS NOT. A name on it is somebody the post office was holding a letter for on 31 March 1835 — good evidence of presence or recent presence, not proof of residence on 1 July, and no evidence at all of a trade or an address. Several entries carry the office's own duplicate count ('Bullen, Jeduthan 2', 'Murry, Alanzo 2', 'Quthet, Daniel 3'), which means more than one letter was waiting and is dropped from the normalized name while staying in the printed form. Three entries are FIRMS and not persons — 'Compart & Coquillard', 'Goodrich & Abell', 'Stephens & Co.' — and they are minted as they stand, because a firm holding mail is a firm doing business here; Goodrich & Abell and the Goodrich of the 1835-06-24 advertising column are very likely the same house and T-0304's firm-merge rule is what should settle that, not this pass.

CROSS-HITS WORTH THE NEXT PASS'S TIME. At least a dozen of these names are also advertisers or officers in the same file — Beaubien, Hugunin, Goodrich, Gooding, Bradstreet, Grant Goodrich, Jasper A. Gooding — and their `letter_list_only` flag will therefore be recomputed to false by the compiler the moment the two readings are merged under T-0299's identity work. That is the compiler's job and nothing is hand-set here.

That is the best anchor in the corpus for the post office itself: Hogan signed the 1 January 1834 letter list as postmaster (T-0310) and the 1835-05-27 marriage notice still calls him 'Postmaster, Chicago Ill.', so the office and his shop stood one door apart on South Water Street through the whole period this pass covers. 'below' IS A DIRECTION AND IT IS NOT RESOLVED HERE. On a street running along a river, 'below' is downstream, which on South Water Street means EAST toward the lake — but the paper never says so, and Chicago usage of the word in 1835 is exactly the sort of thing this corpus should establish rather than assume. The placement records the paper's word and leaves the compass to a later pass with more witnesses.

THE STOCK IS A HARDWARE AND DRY-GOODS STORE'S, and the four tons of Massillon castings — potash and sugar kettles, pots, dish and tea kettles, harrow teeth, stoves — say what a Chicago store's back room actually held.
